provenance.notes: Leaned on the two-buyer pattern: older patients researching slowly and adult children booking for them. No hearing outcomes or device claims; prices, trial terms and credentials stay as clinic-supplied placeholders. Unsure on the manufacturer-programme and buying-group route prices.

pageStructurePlus.section: What happens at a hearing test
pageStructurePlus.contains: Each step of the appointment in order: a chat about everyday listening, an ear check, the sound booth, speech-in-noise listening, and the results explained in plain words, with [duration] for each and a note to bring a family member
pageStructurePlus.why: Many people put off a hearing test because they expect a sales pitch. Seeing the steps, and that results are explained calmly first, is what gets the booking.

pageStructurePlus.section: Hearing aid styles and what's bundled
pageStructurePlus.contains: The hearing aid styles the clinic fits (behind-the-ear, receiver-in-canal, in-the-ear, rechargeable), the clinic's [price bands], and what each includes: fitting, follow-up visits, cleanings and [trial period terms]
pageStructurePlus.why: Buyers compare the total price and what comes with it. Adult children want a number before they let a parent walk into a fitting.

pageStructurePlus.section: Booking a hearing test for a parent or partner
pageStructurePlus.contains: How to book a hearing test for someone else, why the clinic encourages a family member to come along, how consent and sharing of results work, and the parking and step-free access at the door
pageStructurePlus.why: The person searching is often a son, daughter or spouse. A page written to them turns the researcher into the person who books.

pageStructurePlus.contains: What a tinnitus consultation involves, the options the audiologist may discuss in the clinic's approved wording, and what the first visit costs, with no promise of relief
pageStructurePlus.why: Tinnitus searchers are anxious and read late at night. A calm, honest explanation earns the consultation; a promise would lose their trust and break the rules.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Walk-in cleaning hours, repair drop-off and loaner aids, domes, wax guards and batteries by pickup or post, loss and damage cover on the clinic's [terms], and remote adjustment if offered
pageStructurePlus.why: Existing wearers choose a clinic they can rely on for service. Clear aftercare also wins people unhappy with where they bought their aids.

pageStructurePlus.section: Earwax removal and custom ear protection
pageStructurePlus.contains: Earwax removal appointments by the method the clinic uses, custom musician earplugs, swim plugs and noise protection moulds, each with a [price] and booking link
pageStructurePlus.why: Wax removal and custom moulds bring in new faces who often book a hearing test later, so these pages feed the main appointment.

openers.line: Your hearing clinic's Maps listing has kind reviews but no website, so a daughter looking up audiologists for her dad in {City} can't see what a hearing test involves before she calls.
openers.hook: Open their Maps listing and confirm there is no Website button. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Here's what could sit behind that button for the hearing clinic: {demo-link}

openers.line: The website link on your listing opens the audiology clinic's Facebook page. Someone pricing hearing aids wants styles, what's bundled and a test booking, not a feed.
openers.hook: Tap the link on their listing and confirm it lands on Facebook. Note the latest post.
openers.linkLine: The hearing clinic's essentials on one page: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your site still shows hearing aid styles that look several generations old, with no mention of rechargeable aids. Buyers who've read up notice that before they ever call.
openers.hook: Open their site and find one stale detail: an old device range, a departed audiologist, old hours. Note it.

openers.line: I opened your hearing clinic's site on my phone and the text was tiny with no way to tap to call. Your patients' families read on phones, often on behalf of someone older.
openers.hook: Only if they have a site. Load it on your phone and note the text size and the call path. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: The hearing clinic, rebuilt for a phone and easy to read: {demo-link}

openers.line: There's no way to book a hearing test online, only a phone line during clinic hours. Plenty of people with hearing loss find phone calls the hardest part.
openers.hook: Look for any booking form or calendar on their site or listing. If calling is the only route, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: Hearing test booking without a phone call: {demo-link}

openers.line: A lot of hearing test bookings are made by a son or daughter. Nothing on your page speaks to them: how to book for a parent, whether they can come along, what it costs.
openers.hook: Read their reviews for mentions of a family member who booked or came along. Quote one if you find it.
openers.linkLine: A page for families booking a hearing test for a parent: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your Google reviews keep mentioning how patiently the audiologist explains everything. That's what a nervous first-time hearing aid buyer wants to read, and it's not on any page they'd find.
openers.hook: Read their reviews and copy one phrase about patience, explanation or follow-up care. Quote it back. Never imply a hearing result.
openers.linkLine: Your reviews beside the hearing test booking: {demo-link}

openers.line: End-of-year family gatherings are when relatives notice someone missing the conversation. The weeks after are when they search for a hearing test nearby and pick the clinic that explains it best.
openers.hook: Use this in the weeks before the end-of-year holidays or a big local family occasion. Name the occasion.
openers.linkLine: A hearing clinic page ready for after the holidays: {demo-link}

openers.line: People search about ringing in their ears at night, when it's loudest and the clinic is closed. Your page doesn't mention tinnitus consultations or let them request one.
openers.hook: Check whether their site or listing mentions tinnitus at all. If it doesn't, or there's no request route, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A calm tinnitus consultation page for the clinic: {demo-link}

openers.line: Saw the clinic is hiring an audiologist. Candidates compare independent hearing practices partly on how the clinic presents its patients, equipment and team online.
openers.hook: Only if they posted a hiring notice for an audiologist, hearing aid practitioner or front desk. Note the date.
openers.linkLine: A hearing clinic page with a careers section: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your posts mention visiting care homes for hearing checks and aid cleaning. A page listing the residences you visit and how families arrange it would bring you more of that work.
openers.hook: Look for posts about care home visits, home visits or a mobile van. Use the real names they mention.
openers.linkLine: A home and care home visits page for the audiology clinic: {demo-link}

openers.line: Under your posts, people ask what hearing aids cost and whether they can pay monthly. A clear page on price bands and payment options answers it before they talk themselves out of it.
openers.hook: Look for cost or payment questions in comments and reviews. Never state a price or plan they haven't published.
openers.linkLine: Hearing aid prices and payment options on one page: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your audiologist clearly has years of training, and nothing online says which licence or qualifications they hold. That's the first thing a careful hearing aid buyer checks.
openers.hook: Look at their bios and posts for qualifications. Never state a licence, degree or membership they haven't published.

openers.line: It looks like many of your hearing patients come from local family doctors. Each one still looks the clinic up before booking, and finds very little to confirm the referral.
openers.hook: Look for reviews saying 'my doctor sent me' or posts thanking referring practices. Quote it.
openers.linkLine: Where a referred hearing patient would land: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your {specific recent job} post explained hearing aid care better than most clinic sites do. Right now it scrolls away within a week instead of living on a page families can find.
openers.hook: Pick their newest educational post, community talk or clinic event and name it exactly. Never a patient story.
openers.linkLine: That hearing care explanation, on its own page: {demo-link}

Would you like me to send it over?

{Owner}, following up in case my note got lost between appointments. Here's the sample audiology site for {Business Name}: {demo-link}

It walks a first-timer through the hearing test, gives families their own page, and lets people book without phoning, which matters to people who struggle on the phone. If it's not for you, say so and I won't message again.
sequence.call:
"Hi, is this {Owner}? I'm {Your Name}, I build websites for hearing clinics here in {City}. I sent a message a couple of days ago, did it come through?"

IF NO:
"No problem, you're in the booth most of the day. Short version: I built a sample site for {Business Name} with the hearing test explained, a page for families and online booking, with marked placeholders where your photos would go. Can I email you the link?"

IF YES:
"What did you think?"
 → let them talk, don't fill the silence
"The build runs {Build Range}, then {Care Range} a month for hosting and updates. For a clinic like yours I'd normally quote about {Build Price}, which is less than a single pair of hearing aids."
"Its job is to make the hearing test feel safe to book, for the patient and for the son or daughter doing the research."
"Could I take fifteen minutes after your last appointment this week?"

CLOSE:
"I'll send a one-page scope and a deposit invoice. We start the day it clears, and you approve every word before it goes live."

objections.objection: The hearing aid manufacturer already gave us a website.
objections.handler: "Keep their product pages if you like. Their site is a template shared with many clinics and it sells their devices. Yours should sell your audiologist, your aftercare and your test, and it's a domain you own."

objections.objection: Our patients are older, they just phone us.
objections.handler: "Many do. But their children research on phones, and people with hearing loss often find calls hard. Online booking adds a route without taking the phone away."

objections.objection: We don't put hearing aid prices online.
objections.handler: "Then we show price bands and what's bundled, in your words, or a placeholder until you decide. Buyers who see a range book a test; buyers who see nothing assume the worst."

objections.objection: We can't make claims about hearing results.
objections.handler: "Right, and the site doesn't. It explains the appointment, the styles you fit and the aftercare, with no promises. Testimonials only with written consent, and every credential comes from you."

objections.objection: Most of our patients come through a benefits network.
objections.handler: "Keep the network. Those patients still look you up before they choose which listed clinic to visit. The site is what makes them pick yours, and it brings in private-pay buyers too."
"{Build Range}. For your clinic about {Build Price}, because of the test walkthrough, family and aftercare pages. One fitting covers it."

Reply if you'd like me to keep it up a little longer.
sequence.nurture:
Hi {Owner}, the weeks after end-of-year family gatherings are when relatives start booking hearing tests for someone they noticed struggling. Clinics with online booking and a page for families catch more of those.

The sample's still here and the price hasn't changed. {demo-link} if you'd like another look.

bullets: Peg the build to a single pair of hearing aids sold, not to a hearing test fee.
Price the hearing test walkthrough and the family page as core work; they are what turn research into a booking.
Never undercut the manufacturer's free template on price. Sell ownership, the clinic's own voice and aftercare pages.
Leave hearing aid prices, trial terms and credentials as placeholders until the clinic supplies them in writing.
Quote an accessibility pass on every build; this audience reads with larger text and screen readers.
Keep monthly add-ons below the cost of a single repair visit.

lineItems.description: Max with the clinic's price band, what's bundled, rechargeable and connectivity notes, and a book-a-fitting link.
Max when written from an audiologist interview, with each step, its duration, a family member note and placeholders for booth photos.
Max with the clinic's approved wording on options, a separate request route and a review round with the audiologist.

lineItems.item: Separate booking types for test, fitting and wax removal
lineItems.description: Max when each appointment type has its own length, room and audiologist rules pulled from their existing scheduling system.
Max with every dome, wax guard and battery size listed, pickup or post options and a card payment.

lineItems.item: Care home visit page with request form
lineItems.description: Max when it lists the residences visited, visit days and a separate request route for care home staff.
Max when the test walkthrough, family page, aftercare and booking are translated and checked by bilingual staff.

whatElseYouSell.name: Audiologist and sound booth photo session
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "One morning photographing the audiologists, the sound booth, the fitting room and the entrance, with staff as models. Patients appear only with their written consent."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 2, before the style pages fill up with placeholders nobody replaces.

whatElseYouSell.name: Hearing clinic Google profile upkeep
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Weekly posts on the hearing clinic's Google profile about walk-in cleaning hours, wax removal slots and care home visit days, so searches for an audiologist nearby find a current clinic."

whatElseYouSell.name: Review requests after the fitting follow-up
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "After the final fitting follow-up, the patient gets a polite note asking about their experience with the audiologist, never about their hearing or the device."
whatElseYouSell.when: Day 30. Wording approved by the clinic first.

whatElseYouSell.name: Consent and patient photo policy pages
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A privacy notice, a written consent form for testimonials and fitting-day photos, and a page explaining how the hearing clinic stores test results, all in the clinic's approved wording."
whatElseYouSell.when: At build, before any patient story or photo is used.

whatElseYouSell.name: Accessibility review for older and hard-of-hearing visitors
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A full pass on the hearing clinic site for large text, contrast, screen readers, captions on every video and booking that never requires a phone call."
whatElseYouSell.when: At launch, then once a year or after a redesign.

whatElseYouSell.name: Advertising-approval-ready audiology content pack
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Every hearing aid and tinnitus page assembled with its claims checklist, sources the audiologist supplied and placeholders, ready to submit where the regulator requires approval."
whatElseYouSell.when: Before launch, and before any paid ad campaign.

whatElseYouSell.name: Community hearing check day promotion
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A flyer, an event page and posts for the clinic's hearing check mornings at libraries, seniors' clubs and community centres."

whatElseYouSell.name: Printed hearing guide for family doctors' waiting rooms
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A short printed guide on what happens at a hearing test, with the clinic's booking details, for family doctors' waiting rooms and pharmacy counters that agree to stock it."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 3, once the walkthrough page is live.

withoutAI.route: Family doctor practices that refer hearing patients
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The family practice that sends you hearing patients has a site with no online booking. I build careful clinic sites already, and you can introduce me."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Doctors and the audiologist they refer to talk often. The clinic owner's introduction is the warm route in.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The retirement residence where your audiologist runs hearing check mornings has a dated site. A tour booking and activities page would help their families too."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Residence managers already trust the clinic that cares for their residents.

withoutAI.route: Home care agencies with hard-of-hearing clients
withoutAI.whoPays: The agency, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The home care agency whose caregivers bring clients to your hearing clinic is hiring constantly from a bare page. A careers and services site helps them both ways."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Agencies and clinics share elderly clients and swap referrals.

withoutAI.whoPays: The school or studio, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The music school that sends students to you for custom musician earplugs takes enrolments by email. A lesson booking site naming the audiology clinic as its partner suits both."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Musicians' ear protection is a natural tie between the two, and teachers trust the clinic that fitted them.

withoutAI.whoPays: The optometry practice, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The eye care practice next door sees the same older patients as your hearing clinic. An exam booking site for them is a short introduction away."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Eye and hearing practices often cross-refer and sometimes share a building.

withoutAI.whoPays: The support group, from its own funds
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The hearing loss support group that meets at your clinic lists its meetings on a flyer. A small site with captioned meeting notes and a sign-up would help members."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Support groups are run by volunteers who trust the audiologist hosting them.

withAI.route: Appointment logistics assistant for the family practice
withAI.pitchLine: "Patients asking the doctor's office about hours, repeat prescriptions and where to get a hearing test get the practice's approved answers, and medical questions go to staff."
withAI.whyItWorks: Front desks answer the same logistics questions all day. Admin-only answers carry no clinical risk.

withAI.route: Family question assistant for the retirement residence
withAI.pitchLine: "Families asking the residence about visiting times, activities and the next hearing clinic visit day get answers from the residence's own approved pages."
withAI.whyItWorks: Residence offices field family calls around the clock and want fewer interruptions.

withAI.route: Shift fill helper for the home care agency
withAI.pitchLine: "When a caregiver drops a shift, the agency's helper drafts the message to available staff and notes which clients have hearing clinic appointments that week."
withAI.whyItWorks: Last-minute shift gaps are the agency's daily headache.

withAI.route: Lesson enquiry assistant for the music school
withAI.pitchLine: "Parents asking the music school about lesson times, fees and ear protection for drum students get answers from the school's pages, with the hearing clinic named for earplug fittings."
withAI.whyItWorks: Small music schools lose enquiries in the evening when nobody answers.

withAI.route: Recall reminder drafts for the optometry practice
withAI.pitchLine: "The eye care practice's annual exam reminders get drafted in its own voice for staff to send, the same way the hearing clinic's recall notes work."
withAI.whyItWorks: Recall letters are tedious and practices put them off.

withAI.route: Captioned meeting summaries for the support group
withAI.pitchLine: "Each hearing loss support meeting gets a captioned recording and a plain summary for members who missed it, checked by a volunteer before it's shared."
withAI.whyItWorks: Members with hearing loss value written records, and volunteers lack the time to write them.

softwareAI.name: Privacy-safe hearing test booking and hosting setup
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Hearing test and fitting requests come in through a form that asks only for name, contact and appointment type, on hosting set up for the privacy rules where the clinic practises."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: At build. Needs the appointment types, who receives requests and the clinic's privacy wording.

softwareAI.name: Annual hearing check recall
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Patients due for their yearly hearing check get a friendly reminder with a booking link, by email, text or post for those who prefer paper."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Day 30. Needs last test dates from their system, contact consent and the clinic's wording.

softwareAI.name: Battery and wax guard reorder
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Hearing aid wearers reorder batteries, domes and wax guards from the clinic in a few taps, for pickup or post, instead of phoning the front desk."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs the accessory list, prices and a payment account.

softwareAI.name: Fitting follow-up visit reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "New hearing aid wearers get a reminder before each follow-up adjustment visit, and a nudge if the next one isn't booked yet."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs fitting dates from their schedule and the clinic's follow-up pattern. No device or hearing details in messages.

softwareAI.name: Front desk answering while the audiologist is in the booth
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When the only receptionist is helping a patient, calls about hours, wax removal and booking a hearing test get answered; anything about hearing or devices goes to an audiologist."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, once they trust you. Needs approved answers and schedule access. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Hearing clinic review thank-you drafts
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Each hearing clinic review gets a reply drafted for approval that thanks the reviewer without confirming they're a patient or mentioning their hearing aids."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2, alongside the fitting review requests. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Repair and loaner aid tracker
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every hearing aid sent away for repair is tracked as received, shipped, back and collected, with the loaner aid logged against the patient."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their repair steps and loaner stock. Tracks status only; records stay in their own system.

softwareAI.name: Warranty and loss cover expiry alerts
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Wearers get a note before their hearing aid warranty or loss cover ends, with a booking link for a clean and check while it's still covered."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs purchase dates and the clinic's cover terms.

softwareAI.name: Pre-visit listening situations questionnaire
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Before the hearing test, patients note where they struggle, like restaurants, television or phone calls, inside the clinic's secure system, so the audiologist starts prepared."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs the clinic's own questions and a secure form inside their patient system, not the public site.

softwareAI.name: Captions and transcripts for clinic videos
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every hearing aid care video the clinic posts gets accurate captions and a written transcript drafted for staff to check, so the people who need captions most aren't left out."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, once they film aftercare videos. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Family member question assistant
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A son or daughter asking how to book a hearing test for a parent, whether they can come along and what it costs gets the clinic's approved answers and the booking link."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs the family page wording and price bands approved. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Fitting-day care summary drafts
softwareAI.pitchLine: "After a fitting, the audiologist's notes become a plain care sheet on charging, cleaning and the next visit, reviewed by the audiologist inside the clinic's secure system."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6, only inside their secure system. Needs their current care sheet. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Trial period check-in sequence
softwareAI.pitchLine: "During the hearing aid trial, the wearer gets a short check-in asking how they're finding it and whether they'd like an adjustment visit before the trial ends."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs the clinic's trial terms and approved wording.

softwareAI.name: Device and accessory stock board
softwareAI.pitchLine: "See demo hearing aids, loaners, chargers and accessory stock at a glance, with low-stock alerts before a fitting day runs short."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs their stock list and who reorders.

softwareAI.name: Doctor update letter drafts
softwareAI.pitchLine: "After a hearing test for a referred patient, the audiologist's results become a draft letter to the referring doctor, checked and signed inside the clinic's secure system."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6, only inside their secure system. Needs their letter template. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Hearing check day sign-up
softwareAI.pitchLine: "People book a slot at the clinic's community hearing check mornings online and get a reminder the day before, with a large-print option."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4, when they run community events. Needs dates, venues and slot lengths.

softwareAI.name: Remote adjustment request queue
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Wearers ask for a hearing aid adjustment from home, and the audiologist sees a queue with the best time to call, instead of messages scattered across phones."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5, for clinics that offer remote adjustments. Needs their process and contact consent.

softwareAI.name: Hearing care posts drafted from audiologist notes
softwareAI.pitchLine: "The audiologist jots a few lines on cleaning aids or protecting hearing at concerts, and a post in the clinic's voice comes back with any outcome wording flagged."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs past posts and the clinic's do-not-say list. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Second-language reply drafts for the hearing clinic
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A patient writing in another language about hearing test times or battery orders gets a reply in that language, drafted for the front desk to check and send."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5, for clinics with patients who prefer another language. Needs translated wording checked by staff. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Referral source and fitting dashboard
softwareAI.pitchLine: "See which doctors, care homes and searches bring hearing test bookings each month, and how many of those tests lead to a fitting."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 7, once booking and repair data has built up for a few months.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Productise the hearing clinic site for independent audiologists
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I built a hearing test walkthrough, family page and aftercare section for one audiology clinic. Every independent on a manufacturer template needs the same."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Independents compete with retail chains on trust and aftercare, and a site they own is the cheapest way to show it.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Offer member clinics a hearing clinic site template with the test walkthrough and accessibility built in, with placeholders for each member's credentials."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Associations want members to look professional and to reach more of the public.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your independent hearing clinics run identical template sites. A clinic-owned template with your device pages slotted in keeps them loyal and gives each its own voice."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Manufacturers fund marketing for clinics that fit their devices, and want those clinics to win locally.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Buying groups for independent hearing practices
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your member audiologists need sites that don't look like the chains. License my hearing clinic template as a member benefit."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Buying groups compete for members on the benefits they bundle.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Each hearing centre in your network needs local pages for its audiologists, care home visits and parking under one brand. I build one approved template and roll it out."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Networks need every location to look consistent and local at the same time.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: White-label hearing clinic template for healthcare agencies
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your agency builds audiology sites from a general medical template. License mine with the hearing test walkthrough, family page and accessibility pass built in."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Agencies avoid regulated health writing and accessibility work. You sell the hard part.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Ear, nose and throat groups adding audiology
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your group is adding a hearing clinic. It needs its own test, fitting and aftercare pages, which I've already built for an independent audiologist."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Groups adding audiology need a separate front door quickly, and you bring the proof.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Optical retail groups adding hearing services
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your stores are adding hearing tests beside eye exams. Each needs a hearing page with booking and an audiologist bio, and I have the template ready."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Optical groups serve the same older customers and roll services out store by store.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Each hearing clinic you acquire arrives with its own dated site. I move them onto one template and keep each clinic's local audiologist and care home pages."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Roll-ups need consistency fast and buy in batches.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your audiology owner clients all need a site that books hearing tests online. License my hearing clinic template as part of your programme."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Coaches want deliverables for many clinics without building them.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: New audiology clients in a new metro
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Hearing clinics far from {City} don't compete with my client, so they get the same hearing test walkthrough, family page and aftercare structure."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Careful, accessible health wording is slow to write. Reusing it elsewhere is margin.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The clinic leaving its sponsored site
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your hearing clinic site belongs to a device maker's programme and ends if you change suppliers. I move it to a domain you own without losing your pages."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Clinics that switch supplier or go fully independent need a new site quickly and already have the budget.
